/insights/most-cited-brand-wins/.article:
In AI search, the most-cited brand wins. Here's how we became it.

Search4 min readSeptember 10, 2026By Nicole Irmo

Rankings measure where you show up. Citations measure whether you're the answer. That difference decided our category.

In early 2025, Google's AI Overviews started answering questions before anyone scrolled to the results. My spidey sense was tingling. If people were going to get the answer before they saw a single link, ranking wasn't the goal anymore. Being the answer was.

My first move was the classic marketer move. I asked our Google rep when we'd be able to buy ads in AI Overviews, since every promoted placement sat below the magic box. We had to be able to buy our way in, right? He didn't know when, or if, that was coming. If we wanted into the answer, we needed to be the chosen one.

A ranking is a chance to be seen. A citation is being chosen. In a category where the buyer is often a caregiver, tired and asking a very specific question at 11pm, being the answer is worth more than being on the list.

1,291citations, against 986 for the nearest competitor. As of June 2026, the brand is the most-cited domain in its category (source: Scrunch).

Being first has its perks. And its problems.

The first problem: nobody could measure it. Rankings went into the monthly report, but citations, the moments when an assistant actually names your brand, weren't tracked at all. The SEO tools we already used didn't track AI answers yet. We found a tool called Scrunch, layered it into our reporting and put AI citations right next to the search report.

That changed the conversation. The team stopped asking "where do we rank?" and started asking "are we the answer? If not, who is, and why?"

The second problem: the bots made a mess of GA4. The same LLM crawlers we were racing to attract flooded our sessions data. So while we worked to get assistants to crawl and cite us, we also had to figure out how to separate their traffic from real visitors.

What we actually did

Inside the team, AI search became almost a mythical creature. We called it the AI monster, and the strategy was simple: feed the beast. Here's what we fed it.

  • Retrofitted hundreds of our 400+ blog posts. Each one got a key takeaways section up top (a TL;DR for the LLMs) and an FAQ section, because LLMs love a Q&A format.
  • Built authority hubs. Long-form pages designed to be the definitive resource on the topics that matter most to our customers. The kind of page an assistant can reference with confidence.
  • Added schema and structured content. So machines can tell what each page is, what it answers and how the pieces connect.
  • Doubled down on video. We hired a full-time, in-house video producer. The bet: Google loves Google, so YouTube is likely to show up in AI Overviews.

Here's the part people find hard to believe: assistants reward the same clarity people do. If a person can skim your page and get the answer in ten seconds, a model can too. If a person has to wade through preamble, so does the model, and it'll quote someone else.

The three things that made the difference

Moving early. We started before there were tools built for it. Complicated? Yes. Worth it? Also yes.

Structure. Every hub has a clear question at the top, a direct answer beneath it, then the depth. Headings that say what the section is. Tables where a table is honest.

Measurement. We started out chasing AI click-through: traffic from assistants to our site. Then we learned LLM traffic is more of a research step, so clicks aren't the most telling number. Citations are. Content programs die in the gap between "we published it" and "it worked." The right number closes that gap.

Rankings tell you where you stand. Citations tell you whether anyone listened.

What to do this quarter

Pick the ten questions your buyers ask most. Not the ten keywords with the highest volume. The ten questions a real person would ask a knowledgeable friend. Answer each one better than anyone in your category, in plain language, on a page you own.

Then go back through what you've already published. Add a TL;DR and an FAQ to your top posts. It's the fastest win on the list.

Then start counting citations. Ask the major assistants your ten questions once a month and record who gets named. Don't judge it by clicks. It isn't perfect measurement. It's good enough to see a trend, and a trend is what you need to keep the program funded.

And before you trust your sessions data, check how much of it is bots.

If nobody in your company is counting citations yet, that's the opening. It was ours.

Up next

We're prepping for agentic shopping. Because if Claude can plan my Christmas trip and map out how to max my credit card reward points, it can surely buy adult diapers.

/insights/hire-seven-of-nine/.article:
Seven of nine: building a marketing team that stays

Team3 min readAugust 27, 2026By Nicole Irmo

One voluntary departure in three and a half years isn't luck. It's a few unglamorous decisions, made on purpose.

I hired seven of the nine people on today's marketing and ecommerce team. My first hire was in social media. Three years later, she's been promoted twice. In three and a half years, one person has chosen to leave.

7 of 9hired, 3 promoted, 1 voluntary departure.

People assume there's a trick. There isn't. A team that stays isn't something you fix at the exit interview. It starts before anyone's hired, and it runs on a handful of decisions that are easy to describe and hard to keep.

It starts with the job description

My job descriptions are long, on purpose. They spell out what success looks like in the role. In interviews, I'm up front about our warts. Nobody should find them in month three and feel misled.

When candidates ask what I'm looking for, my answer is always the same: someone who drinks our Kool-Aid. I want to work with people who are excited about our mission. You can't teach someone to care, and I don't want to work with anyone who doesn't.

I also hire for different personality types. Our customers aren't a monolith, and our team can't be either. You need someone on the red team. You need someone who sees what you don't.

Clarity from day one

Every new hire gets a job scorecard, their roadmap to success. They get our team expectations doc, and a guide to working with me: how I communicate, and what I need from them.

From there, everyone owns a written annual strategy with KPIs they helped define. People stay where they can see their own scoreboard. When they can point at a number and say "that one's mine and it moved," they stay to move it again.

When in doubt, write it out

We document everything. Plans, decisions, how things get done. Writing it down is how a team runs without waiting on one person.

We're also as transparent as we can be. Leaders can't let the team in on everything, but the more we share, the more trust we earn.

And there are no bad ideas. It's a cliché, and we live by it anyway. Some of my favorite campaigns sounded crazy in the room until we found the workable take.

Every quarter, everyone, from graphics to content to web development, presents their own results and learnings. Not to report. To think out loud about what worked and what's next.

On the team, not above it

I'm willing to get my hands dirty. If someone brings me work that's 90% there, that's an A. Adding the last 10% is my job.

When someone makes a mistake, we fix the problem first. Then we figure out what we learned. It's easy to take accountability when the result is help, not blame.

ABC: always be coaching

Feedback is a gift, so my team gets it regularly, and it goes both ways. But coaching is more than feedback. It's making room for the conversations that help people grow. That's why, once a month, I take someone from the team out to lunch, one-on-one, because the honest conversation happens away from the desk. It's why skip-level access stays open, so nobody feels trapped under one relationship. And it's why I say yes to the conference, the course, the stretch project, even when the quarter is tight. The cost of a departure is always higher than the cost of the course.

Coaching also means noticing when things go right. That's where Friday stand-ups come in, because adults need applause too. Saying "good job" and "thank you" costs nothing and can mean everything.

A team that stays compounds. A team that leaves sends you back to the start.

The cost of doing this

It's slower. Documenting, onboarding and coaching take time you could spend shipping. There are weeks I'd rather just do the thing myself. But if I'm the only one who can do it, I haven't done my job. My job is building a team that can do it without me.

/insights/story-sells/.article:
Story sells: turning a 20-year-old product marketplace into a brand

Brand3 min readAugust 12, 2026By Nicole Irmo

Twenty years in business, twenty years online and no story anyone could repeat. Here's how a marketplace became a brand.

For its first 20 years, the company was a marketplace: a one-stop shop for medical supplies. When it started designing its own products, it kept operating like one. The thinking was very Field of Dreams: if you build it, they will come.

Then the company stopped selling competitors' brands to focus on its own. The catalog got smaller, and it wasn't the convenient place to buy the brands customers already knew anymore. It had to stand for something on its own.

The great news: it did. The company's values and core operating principles were on every wall in the building. They just weren't on any of its web pages.

When I joined, marketing meant website support. There were great products and no story. That isn't a marketing problem. It's a story problem, and you can't fix a story problem with a bigger ad budget. So I led the charge to tell it.

Listen first

We didn't start by writing. We started by listening. We read customer reviews and talked to our customer service team, the people who hear from customers every day. Why did this product matter so much to them? What was the emotional way in?

We also acknowledged the suck. Positivity is great, but the human experience is multifaceted, and no one is excited to buy adult diapers. So we chose honest and real. We wanted to feel like a friend, not a company.

Then build the story

What we heard shaped the positioning: who the product is for, what it does that nothing else does, and why that matters to someone who'd rather not think about it at all. Then we wrote the voice: honest, real and human. Then a messaging architecture with standards for each stage of the funnel, so a product page, a TV spot and a customer email all sound like the same company.

A brand people cite, share and buy from isn't built by producing more. It's built by deciding what to say and then saying it everywhere.

Bring the storytellers in-house

If the story is the strategy, the storytellers can't be on loan. Our social media was run by an agency. We decided it was a key storytelling platform and brought it in-house. Freelance blog writers became in-house content managers.

Then we scaled, from ad hoc requests to 40+ published pieces a month. Volume is easy once you know what you're saying. Volume before you know is just noise, and expensive noise.

Say it everywhere

The product page answers the same questions the ad raised. The email after an order sounds like the person who wrote the ad, not a shipping system. The blog, the video and social all tell one story from different angles.

Consistency is boring to talk about, and it's the entire game. Every place the story is told slightly differently is a place the customer has to reconcile it, and customers don't do that work. They leave.

From story to movement

A good story works on new customers and loyal ones. Loyal customers become advocates, and advocates tell the story for you. That's the flywheel.

So we stopped just telling the story and started building a movement:

  • A customer hero club that captured 500 customer stories.
  • A fan event. For a medical product.
  • A brand ambassador program in a category most people can't even name.

Turns out people will talk about adult diapers. You just have to give them a reason.

The results followed the story

Organic search grew 32% in a year the industry declined 2.5%. Conversion on blog traffic went from 3.1% to 15.3%, because the blog stopped being a library and became part of the store. Revenue grew 53% in under three years.

+53%revenue in under three years.

I want to be careful about causality. The story didn't sell the product by itself. Great products sold the product. What the story did was remove the friction between someone having a problem and understanding, quickly, that this was the answer.

If you're turning a marketplace into a brand

Listen before you write. Your reviews and your customer service team already know more of the story than you think.

Write the story before you redesign. A redesign without a position is expensive decoration.

Bring your storytellers in-house. The people telling your story every day should know it by heart.

Then say it everywhere, including the places nobody thinks of as marketing. The packing slip. The hold music. The way the phone is answered.

And check your walls. Your story might already be hanging there.

/insights/community-where-nobody-talks/.article:
Building community in a category where customers rarely speak up

Community3 min readMay 28, 2026By Nicole Irmo

Most brands won't even say "adult diapers." We found more than 500 customers willing to share their stories anyway.

Most brands in our category won't say "adult diapers." They say briefs, or underwear, or anything that sounds a little less like what it is. We found more than 500 customers willing to say, out loud, "I wear adult diapers."

Community marketing usually starts with fans who already love you in public. Ours don't. Nobody tags their adult diapers in a vacation photo. When your best customers are also your quietest, the classic playbook of finding fans and amplifying them has nothing to amplify.

So we built this community the only way that works in a private category: slowly, one brave step at a time, with each step asking a little more of us and a little more of our customers.

Go first

You can't ask customers to show their faces if you won't show yours. So our team went on camera first, talking about adult diapers in our own voices. Before anyone else would trust the brand, they needed proof there were real people behind it.

Next, we needed someone outside the company to take the leap with us. Our first influencer was a twentysomething with bright pink hair and MS who was already talking openly about incontinence. Afterward, VICE called her the world's first adult diaper influencer.

Go slow

Our first call for customer video stories brought in three. It sounds small. At the time, it felt like a breakthrough.

So we raised the stakes. I'd been looking for a reason to give away a year's supply of diapers, and a story contest was it: customers would share their experiences, and other customers would pick the winner. I was hoping for 100. More than 500 people entered. Our customers had plenty to say. They'd just never been asked the right way. That contest became the basis for our customer hero club.

500+customer stories, from a contest where I hoped for 100.

Get braver

Every yes made the next ask easier. We launched a brand ambassador program shortly after and were buried in applications. Then we did something that still makes me grin: we threw a fan event. For adult diapers.

Over two weekends, more than 40 longtime customers traveled in from California, Idaho, Florida, Connecticut, New York and beyond. They cruised the Chicago River, cheered at Wrigley and ate their weight in deep-dish. Then they toured the warehouse, tested products side by side and gave our leadership team their unfiltered feedback.

Why they show up

None of these people are in it for money or followers. They remember how long it took to find the right product and the right support, and they want to make that search shorter for the next person.

The numbers

Engagement grew 144% year over year, to record levels. Followers climbed from 35,400 to 56,600 across eight platforms, and monthly follower growth hit 4.47%, against platform benchmarks of 0.3% to 1.4%.

Silence isn't absence. It's a room that hasn't been built yet.

Every category has a version of this: a product people need and never talk about. The playbook doesn't change. Go first. Go slow. Get a little braver every time.
